en: Gaṇacakravidhi (ascribed to Ratnākaraśānti), including the *Saṃkṣiptā Pañjikā* Transcription based on Péter-Dániel Szántó, 2019, “Minor Vajrayāna texts V: The Gaṇacakravidhi attributed to Ratnākaraśānti. In: Nina Mirnig, Marion Rastelli, Vincent Eltschinger (eds.), *Tantric Communities in Context*, Vienna: Austrian Academy of Sciences, pp. 275–314. Manuscript: NAK 5-7871, NGMPP B 104/10.
Tibetan translation: D 1995, rgyud, mi 190v4–192r5 (The Tibetan text here is based on the ACIP electronic edition and has not been compared with manuscripts of the sDe dge canon).
Prepared by Ryan Conlon, March 2021. (Note: I have normalized orthography and incorporated emendations suggested in Szántó 2019.
Homage to Vajrasattva!
Having first prostrated to Vajrasattva, the all-pervading lord who consists of both existence and non-existence, the god who grants all desires, I shall describe the maṇḍala of the Gaṇas. (1)
The mantra-practitioner is devoted to the non-conceptual, ever-collected in meditative absorption,
knowledgeable in the sequence of all tantras, and the best among those who know the ten principles.
With minds moistened by the profound and vast Dharma,
free from pride, and skilled in service, [he was attended] by excellent disciples.
In this secluded and delightful abode, crowded with hosts of deities and bestowing the fruits of the five desires, one should commence one's own worship. || 4 ||
Veneration and worship are prescribed according to the order of seniority;
alternatively, they may be based on the greatness of one's virtues or the honor due to a guest.
One should begin the Gaṇamaṇḍala by offering, according to one's ability, a bath, perfumes, garments, garlands, ornaments, ointments, an arghya offering, and incense.
This is declared to be the action-vajrī mudrā for one who is composed;
having placed a finger to the ear and then to the head, the giver should bow with eight limbs.

Having offered the bali-oblation contained in vessels of jewels and other precious materials, one who is intent upon reality should worship the supramundane Victors and the mundane deities of mantra. (8)
By means of the application of the intended purpose of the mantra, having recited the mantra over the great nectar in the lotus-vessel and over the ten hooks, one should satisfy them all.
Abiding in the state of great bliss, the leader of the assembly should perform all common offerings and all the secret ones, each more sublime than the last. (10)
A woman disciplined and composed, with a lotus-face bowed in humility,
vast in her great virtues and truly fit for the ultimate reality;
free from conceptual constructions in her heart, she is adorned with every ornament.
With her pair of very broad breasts, she held a vessel of loveliness.
Having himself kindled the fuel of the body with the seven-flamed fire of gnosis,
he should cast the mercury and other substances into the mouth and other openings for the sake of the oblation of reality.
Then, [one should meditate upon] the Great Lord Bindu-deva situated in the center of the moon within the heart,
or else one's own chosen deity (iṣṭadeva) and others, adorned with the ornaments of the [spiritual] wheels (cakras).

With the tips of the ring finger, thumb, and middle finger, one should bathe the Sun, whose splendor has been churned by the three principles (tattvas), with streams of nectar-like water placed upon the very tip of the tongue.
Having repeatedly drawn up that essence by means of the sounds (nāda) arising from the navel-cakra, and having drunk it from the three pills, the great yogi may dwell in bliss. 15.
Vimūmāraśu, and another, the five [syllables] of the fire-cow-pit (dahana-gokupa), as well as the Mahāmṛta, are proclaimed in various Tantras and within the Tantras. 16.
One should offer the *chiḍiṅga* from all sides to that [deity] situated in the intermediate space—to the Hero for the Heroic God and for the entire host of goddesses. (17)

Having obtained the reality consisting of the ten goads for the sake of purifying the minds of the donors, one should offer it in its entirety, including both the partial and the complete, to the external deity. || 18 ||

For the sake of accomplishing the state of perfect buddhahood for all beings, one who possesses the power of compassion should worship the Universal Monarch with hymns accompanied by the vajra and bell. 19.
Having thus presented the vessel of food offerings with a gesture of erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*),
[one offers] either each one individually or all as a single unit, through the various combinations of pure and impure elements.
With foods and drinks as desired, and with various multitudes of offerings, the giver of the vajra-holders may speak according to his pleasure and as he wishes. (21)
Thus, free from conceptual construction, like a lion, fearless,
established in the state of peace amidst existence, and endowed with the true nature of reality,
one whose wisdom is equal to one's own heart should sing the *kaiśikī* and other melodies.
One should worship the entire multitude of the hosts of Jinas even while dancing. || 22 ||
He from whose hand the bowl should fall during the successive movements of the hands, whether through delusion or out of contempt, shall be one who incurs the penalty for showing disrespect. 23.

If someone acts through deeds of mind, speech, or body arising from a lack of discipline, it is appropriate to impose a punishment upon him for the sake of pacifying the "boil" and other such afflictions. (24)
The best among those who know the ritual, having performed the mutual gratification with both hands through mudrās according to the rules, [engaged] in festivals of the essence of playful sport.
One who is intent upon reality should honor [the deity] with profound and noble discourses, and with songs, instrumental music, dances, and the supreme means and wisdom. (26)
With mutual respect and with diligent service toward one another,
the practitioner of the vow, a knower of sacrifice, should perform the sacrifice through the applications of the ten perfections.
Having asked for forgiveness, even if he wishes to depart, he should go before him with palms joined;
having accomplished his task, the wise man should enter again, restrained and bowed low. (28)
Always becoming one whose self is yoga, always devoted to reality,
and always perfected in discipline, one should always practice the wheel.
The mudrā of heroes is considered common, like cooked food;
therefore, one who desires [the goal] without remainder should worship both herself and the other. 30.
As long as one’s own will is constant bliss through the play of reality,
so long should one perform the worship of one's own true nature with this very wisdom.

Through the great means of the eyes and other senses, and through the hosts of women such as Rūpā and Lalanā, one should constantly manifest great bliss by means of consciousness in the external world. || 32 ||
[He sees] the splendor of the vajra-lotus, white as the moon, most radiant,
emitting rays of light that are the multitudes of Jinas— devoid of intrinsic nature, yet the very nature [of reality].
With wisdom and command, that excellent being sports in a manner exceedingly delightful through the purity of his countenance toward all sentient beings.
Then, when the time for dismissal arrived, having praised all the gods and the [divine] wheels with auspicious songs and hymns in their presence, || 34 ||
Having sprinkled water upon the donors and joined them with the vow of the Victorious One, he established all beings in unsurpassed Buddhahood. (35)
Having satisfied the Ucchiṣṭadevas and having offered the great bali-oblation,
the wise man, becoming one whose nature is dharma and knowledge, should apply his mind to what is auspicious.

Having meditated upon the Jina, the abode of Dharma, as subtle as a mere thumb's breadth above [the head], one should contemplate him as flowing from that [place] like an infinite stream of nectar into oneself. (37)
In the center of this sky of the heart is the orb of the unbroken moon;
there, one should always contemplate a subtle vajra merged with the Dharma. One should visualize that vajra as being the size of a barley grain. (39)
Endowed with the aesthetic flavors (rasas) such as compassion, consisting of the three liberations, composed of mind, joined with all aspects of meaning, it is immutable great bliss. || 40 ||
The yogin, whose nature consists of wisdom and skillful means, intent upon reality, should in every way and in all activities contemplate the true form of the awakened mind (saṃbodhicitta). 41.
One should contemplate, according to reality, the Bindu— which is radiant by its very nature, recited with the syllables of the Prāṇa-mantra, and liberated from both merit and demerit.
Whether at that time or at all times, one who is devoted to the exertion for liberation and practices constantly shall attain the perfection of liberation.
Having thoroughly honored with all forms of giving and so forth that which is supreme to the desires of the worlds,
and having ground the city of delusion consisting of all conceptual constructions by means of the vajra of selflessness and other methods—
he who turns the wheel of the Guru, the Jina, which brings about the arising of primordial wisdom and bestows liberation.
For the sake of the constant and intense welfare of that great noble one who is devoted to compassion. || 44 ||
To the one who possesses profound qualities for the sake of virtue, who removes the afflictions acquired through conceptual construction and imagination,
and who is liberated from dwelling in latent predispositions; to the one who has attained liberation.
Homage be to the yogin for the sake of the manifestation of the state beyond phenomena. || 45 ||
She who, with her slender form adorned by ornaments, shines like the crescent moon in the sky of the discus,
performs a multitude of deeds.
Homage be to that host of Lalanās! || 46 ||
Having visualized the Teacher of the World, who possesses the wheel, together with the mundane world for the sake of the liberation of all beings,
he who, with a benevolent intention, emulates the maṇḍala—
Homage be to that sovereign of the assembly! || 47 ||
The mass of great bliss arising from the cultivation of the stainless state of all sentient beings' destinies;
the sublime, vast, and condensed ultimate benefit for others.
Together with my wife, I have accomplished everything. || 48 ||
The ritual procedure for the *gaṇacakra* is completed.
Homage to the Buddha. Diplomatic edition of the fragmentary gloss: || namo buddhāya || ||

For those who have been consecrated in the tantras and are engaged in the various modes of conduct (*caryā*), since accomplishment (*siddhi*) does not occur without the performance of the *gaṇacakra*, this is a brief manual (*pañjikā*) on the procedure for the *gaṇacakra*, preceded by prostrations to one’s own chosen deity, the Great Vajradhara, for the purpose of dispelling obstacles and attaining great accomplishment.

[ad 1] First, regarding the term *vajrasattva*: it refers to the ultimate being (*paramārthasattva*) who is indivisible and endowed with reality, whose nature consists of both existence and non-existence. He is the all-pervading lord (*vibhu*) in the forms of the conventional and the ultimate. Because he is joined with the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*), he is "one who possesses all desires" (*sarvakāma*); he bestows that which grants all desires, namely great bliss (*mahāsukha*), and is thus called the "bestower of all desires" (*sarvakāmaprada*). He is a "god" (*deva*) because he shines (*divyati*). Having first prostrated to him, I shall speak—that is, I will explain—the *gaṇamaṇḍala*, the mandala of the pair consisting of the *yoga* and the *yoginī*.

[Regarding verse 2: "Devoted to the non-conceptual" means having a non-conceptual nature (*nirvikalpasvabhāva*). A "mantrin" is one who possesses the mantra (*maṃtra*). "Always concentrated" means being concentrated in that very essence while sitting, walking, performing actions, lying down, sitting, engaging in sexual union, and so forth; knowing how to follow all tantras; following the tantras without exception; and knowing the procedure for the ten principles (*daśatatva*). As for "the ten principles": [text continues].

1. One who has received the outer and secret initiations; 2. one purified of conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*); 3. one who knows the outer and secret maṇḍalas; 4. one skilled in solitude (*viveka*) and meditative absorption (*samādhi*); 5. one who delights in the conduct of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-caryā*); 6. one who knows all the movements of coming and going regarding mudrās and so forth, as well as the application of all ritual actions (*sarvakarma*); 7. one who initiates recitation (*japa*), fire-offerings (*homa*), and worship (*pūjā*); 8. one who is completely liberated from all craving (*tṛṣṇā*); 9. one who teaches the Dharma according to the respective spheres of [the disciples']; 10. one who knows the method of non-dual equality (*advaya-samatā*). Such a yogi should undertake the maṇḍala of the assembly (*gaṇamaṇḍala*); this is the connection [of the verse].

[Regarding 4: Crowded with hosts of deities, filled with young women devoted to the true nature of reality (*tattvasadbhāva*), engaged with the five sense objects such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, secluded, devoid of wicked people, delightful, and charming—in this very *tantra*, they are to be worshipped. One should commence the worship of the ultimate truth (*paramārthapūjā*). The meaning is that one should perform it.

[Regarding 5: Veneration and worship are considered to follow the order of seniority. Veneration, worship, and so forth should be performed according to the sequence of seniority based on initiation (*abhiṣeka*) and consecration (*dīkṣā*). Alternatively, it may be based on the greatness of qualities (*guṇamāhātmya*) due to the excellence of those qualities, or out of respect for the status of a guest (*atithitva*); for one who has arrived from another land is a guest. [Regarding 6: Bathing, perfumes, garlands, clothing, ornaments, and ointments, as well as incense—according to one's ability, one should commence the *gaṇamaṇḍala*. According to one's ability, using whatever is available, the *gaṇacakra* should be performed. The remainder is easy to understand.

[Regarding verse 7: This ritual action of Karmavajrī is taught for one who is concentrated in meditation. With palms joined at the ear and head bowed, for the sake of removing distractions of body, speech, and mind, one should perform the yoga-act of Karmavajrī by placing the joined palms upon each of the heads of the assembly; it should be performed at the ear. Afterwards, the giver bows down before the eight-spoked wheel.

[Regarding verse 8: Having placed the *bali* offering—consisting of food and other items—within a vessel of jewels or the like, one who is intent on reality (*tatvatatpara*) should first offer it to the supramundane Victors, such as the Tathāgatas and others, and afterwards worship the mundane deities, such as Hari, Hara, and Hiraṇyagarbha, as well as the mantra-deities and the obstructing spirits of fields and so forth. One who knows the ritual procedure for reality (*tatvavidhānajña*) should thus perform the worship.

[ad 9] By means of the application of the intended meaning of reality (*tattvābhiprāya*) and according to the sequence of the *samāja* tantra, one should satisfy all those hosts (*gaṇa*). Having recited over the great nectar (*mahāmṛta*) in a lotus vessel, and the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and so forth in vessels such as skull-cups, and having first consecrated the hook (*aṅkuśa*) and the ritual grass (*kuśa*) of the pledge (*samaya*), making them purified by mantra, they should be offered. They must be given.

[ad 10] All are common, worthy of worship, and the cause for attaining the happiness of the entire world; they are the supreme secret of all secrets, the most profound mystery among all ultimate truths. Abiding in the state of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), and abiding in the state of the equal flavor of wisdom and means (*prajñopāya-samarasa*), they exist as the leaders of the assembly. [ad 11] That universal monarch is accompanied by women who are disciplined and modest, women whose lotus-faces are bowed, whose lotus-faces are slightly inclined, who are vast with extensive virtues, endowed with exceedingly broad qualities, and who are fit for reality through reality itself.
